t01-apar-1: CHART No. 1 The School. — The Secondary School. — The Classroom.
t01-01-1: 1. — This chart shows a **classroom** in a **secondary school**. In this classroom there are eight **tables** (18) and eight **benches** (32) . Three pupils sit on each bench. The **teacher** (7) sits on a **chair** (8) at his **desk** (6) .
t01-02-1: 2. — To the left of the desk stands a glass-fronted **cabinet** (15) . To the right is the **blackboard** (1) with the **cloth** (2) and the **chalk** (3) .
t01-02-2: Above the desk hang **wall charts** ( 9 , 11 , 12 ) and a **map** (10) .
t01-03-1: 3. — Not all the pupils are in their **seats** (17) . John (4) is standing at the board; he is holding the cloth and wiping off the **geometrical figures**.
t01-03-2: Peter is near the desk; he is collecting the **written exercises** (5) and bringing them to the teacher.
t01-04-1: 4. — This teacher is the teacher of **modern languages**. He teaches the pupils to speak, read and write foreign languages **(German, English, Spanish, Italian, Russian** or **French)**.
t01-05-1: 5. — The classroom is very large and very bright. At the far end there is a wide **window** with two **transom windows** (78) and a **glazed door** to air it and light it.
t01-05-2: This classroom is not cold. In the middle, to heat it, there is a very good **stove** (46) with its **pipe** (45) .
t01-05-3: **Coat hooks** (58) are fixed to the partition; the pupils’ hats and coats hang from them.
t01-06-2: **Break** (76) has just ended and the lesson is starting again. Break is held in the **yard** (75) . We can see a few pupils playing. An **assistant master** (74) is supervising them.
t01-07-1: 7. — In the yard we can also see various other people: the **inspector** (73) , the **headmaster** (71) and the **deputy head** (72) .
t01-07-2: The inspector inspects the schools, the headmaster runs the school, the deputy head oversees the pupils’ work.
t01-07-3: The fourth figure is the **caretaker** (77) . He is carrying a register under his arm to record the absentees.
t01-08-1: 8. — At the far end of the yard are the **gymnastic apparatus** (70) and the workshop for **handicrafts** (69) .
t01-08-2: To the right of the chart we can just make out the **classrooms** for **music** and **drawing**.
t01-09-1: 9. — The pupils on the first bench to the right of the desk are **Henry** (*) , **Stephen** and **Charles**.
t01-09-2: Henry is very attentive and hard-working; he is listening to the teacher. On his table he has an **exercise book** (28) , a **book** (29) , a **dictionary** (30) and a **pencil case** (31) . His book has many **pages**; each chapter contains several **paragraphs** and each **line** many **words**.
t01-09-4: His neighbor Stephen (24) is keen. He is writing down in his exercise book the lesson set for next time. He has fine **handwriting**. His book is closed. We can see only the **cover** (27) . Beside him lies his pair of **compasses** (26) .
t01-09-5: Charles (23) is holding his book in his hand; he is opening it to go over his lesson again. Like every pupil, he has an **inkwell** (25) in front of him. He is obedient.
t01-10-1: 10. — At the next table are **Louis, Anthony** and **Paul**. Louis is reciting his **lesson** (22) and answering the teacher’s **questions**. Anthony (21) is very inattentive; sometimes the teacher even punishes him. Paul (20) is a good friend, pleasant and obliging. He is very attentive.
t01-11-1: 11. — Behind Henry sits **George** (38) . He is not a bad lad, but he is **talkative**, inattentive and fidgety. His **frivolity** and **disobedience** cause **disruption** during the lesson, and he often deserves a stern **warning**. His **rough book** (35) is dirty, he covers it with **ink blots** from his **pen** (34) , which is why he always uses his **eraser** (36) ; his **satchel** (33) is torn, because he is very careless. Why does he bring his **pencil holder** (37) to the modern languages classroom?
t01-11-2: His neighbor Edmund (39) does not like him. He is admittedly a little lazy, but he is quiet and still. He does not chatter; only, instead of listening, he prefers to read the **stories** in his **reader**.
t01-11-3: The third pupil on this bench is **Ludovic** (40) . He is diligent. He is writing on a white **sheet of paper**. In front of him he has laid his **blotting paper** (41) .
t01-12-1: 12. — The pupils on the second bench, to the teacher’s left, are very young. The first, little **Emil**, cannot write well yet; he brings his **slate** (42) , his **slate pencil** and his **sponge** (43) .
t01-12-2: Next to him are **Augustus** and **Bernard** (44) . The latter works well, but his **appearance** is very untidy.
t01-13-1: 13. — Behind them sit three **idlers**. **Albert** does not learn his lessons. **James** (47) is asleep instead of listening. His **idleness** earns him **reprimands** and even **punishments**. Lastly **Christian** (48) is far too flippant. He **behaves** badly and makes no effort to mend his ways.
t01-14-1: 14. — Their neighbors, by contrast, are well behaved. **Ernest** (51) likes order and regularity; he always uses his **ruler** (50) and his **pencil** (49) . He is a **day pupil**.
t01-14-2: **Francis** (52) is a **boarder**; he wears the uniform, and eats and sleeps at the school. He is a good **friend**.
t01-14-3: Maurice is sharpening his **pencil** with his **penknife** (56) ; he is very careful.
t01-14-4: He brings all his books, his **grammar** (55) , his **notebook** (54) , and even a **writing pad** (53) . His **school bag** (57) is on the floor behind him.
t01-14-5: The two tables at the back of the classroom are taken by **good pupils** (19) .
t01-15-1: 15. — In the **drawing class** there are fine **models** hung on the wall and a **lamp** (62) with a **shade**, hanging from the ceiling. The **teacher** (60) is very patient; he corrects the pupils’ **drawings** (61) and teaches them to draw a **bust** (59) from life.
t01-16-1: 16. — The **music room** looks very interesting. There you learn to read **music**, to sight-sing the **scale notes** (67) written on the **stave** (do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si = C. D. E. F. G. A. B.), to recognise the **clefs** and to sing beautiful **melodies**. The scores are placed on the **music stand** (65) . One of the pupils is **playing the piano** (64) and the **music teacher** (66) is **beating time** (68) .
t01-17-1: 17. — We can just see a corner of the **workshop** for **handicrafts** (69) , where the boys can learn to plane wood and file iron. Not every school has one.
t01-18-1: 18. — The mathematics teacher teaches the pupils **geometry,** **arithmetic, calculation** and the **metric system**. On the chart we can see the main geometrical figures: a **circle** (a) , a **square** (b) , a **triangle** (c) , a **line** (d) .
t01-18-2: We can also see a **sum**; it is not an **addition**, nor a **subtraction**, nor a **multiplication**: it is a **division** (e) .
t01-19-1: 19. — On the metric system chart we can see: a **meter** (a) , a **balance** (b) and its **weights**, a **liter** (e) , a **decaliter** (f) , a **deciliter** and a **cubic meter** (d) .
t01-19-2: The pupils also study **natural science** (11) — zoology (a) , botany (b) , geology (c) — and **history** (12) .
t01-19-3: In the cabinet are the instruments for **physics** (15) and for **chemistry** (16) .
t01-19-4: On top of the cabinet are: a **sphere** (14) , a **cone** and a **globe** (13) .
t01-19-5: Above the charts hangs a **map** showing the five parts of the world: **Europe** (e) , **Asia** (g) , **Africa** (f) , **America** ( a b ) and **Oceania** (h) , and the two great oceans, the **Pacific** (c) and the **Atlantic** (d) .
t02-apar-1: CHART No. 2 The Human Body. — Break. — Games.
t02-tit-0: The Human Body. *(A simple natural science lesson.)*
t02-01-1: 1. — The main parts of the human body are: the **head**, the **trunk** and the **limbs**.
t02-02-1: 2. — The head has two parts: the **skull**, which holds the **brain** and is covered by the **hair**, and the **face**.
t02-03-1: 3. — In our drawing we can see neither the skull nor the brain; but we can see the important parts of the face very clearly.
t02-04-1: 4. — First comes the **forehead**, which suggests a powerful intellect and a mind always at work. The **temples** are very open. The **eye** is lively and wide open. A thick **eyebrow** and long **eyelashes** shield it.
t02-05-1: 5. — Then come the **nose** and the **nostrils**. We use the nose to smell and to breathe. On either side of the nose are the **cheeks**, and further out the **ears**. The lower part of the face consists of the **mouth** and the **chin**.
t02-06-1: 6. — We cannot see them very well, because the **mustache** and the **beard** hide them from us. But we know that the mouth has the two **lips**, the **upper jaw** and the **lower jaw** with their **teeth**, and the **tongue**. With the mouth we speak and eat. With the tongue we taste our food.
t02-07-1: 7. — The eye, the ear, the nose and the mouth are, together with the fingers, the organs of the five senses: **sight**, **hearing**, **smell**, **taste** and **touch**.
t02-08-1: 8. — The head is therefore one of the most interesting parts of the human body.
t02-09-1: 9. — The **neck** joins the head to the trunk. It includes the **throat** and the **nape**.
t02-10-1: 10. — The trunk also holds many essential organs. In the **chest** are the **lungs**, with which we breathe, and the **heart**, which is the center of life. When the heart stops beating, the living creature dies.
t02-12-1: 12. — The other parts of the trunk are the **side**, the **back**, the **shoulders** and the **abdomen** (belly). We lie on our side or on our back to sleep, and we carry loads on our shoulder.
t02-13-1: 13. — In the abdomen are the **stomach** and the **intestines**. They are what digests our food.
t02-14-1: 14. — We have four **limbs**: two **arms** and two **legs**. With our arms we take, hold, lift and gather up objects; with our legs we stand, walk and run.
t02-15-1: 15. — The **shoulder** joins the arm to the body. A very sturdy **muscle**, the biceps, moves the arm, which the **elbow** joins to the **forearm**. The **wrist** forms the joint of the **hand**, which ends in the **fingers** and the **nails**. On the hand we can make out a **vein** (and an artery) in which the **blood** flows.
t02-16-1: 16. — The parts of the leg are: the **thigh**, the **knee** and the **back of the knee**, the **calf**, whose **flesh** is covered by the **skin**, the **ankle** and the **foot**. The **bones** of the leg are very thick and very strong. At the end of the foot are the **toes**. The other parts are the **sole** and the **heel**.
t02-17-1: 17. — That is a nearly complete description of the human body.
t02-17-2: *Note.* — *With the help of the phrase “my ... hurts (my head, and so on)”, the teacher can go over this whole vocabulary again from the point of view of good or bad* **bodily health**.
t02-tit-4: Gymnastics. *(Told by one of the pupils.)*
t02-18-1: 18. — To be supple, nimble and healthy, we must exercise our legs and our arms. That is why we play games and do **gymnastics**.
t02-19-1: 19. — During the week these two exercises take place in the school yard (see chart No. 1). But on Thursdays and Sundays we go out to a large lawn, where we have room to run and enjoy ourselves.
t02-20-1: 20. — Our teachers and our parents sometimes come with us; but it is the **gymnastics teacher** (12) who directs the exercises.
t02-21-1: 21. — On the lawn, to the left of the entrance, stands the **gymnastic apparatus** (1) : we climb the **ladder** (2) , we swing upside down on the **rings** (3) and on the **trapeze** (4) , we haul ourselves up hand over hand to the top of the **rope ladder** (5) or of the **knotted rope** (6) .
t02-22-1: 22. — Meanwhile our friends are vaulting over the **wooden horse** (7) or the **parallel bars** (11) . Others are **boxing** (8) or **fencing** (9) with a mask and a **foil**. Others, finally, are lifting **dumbbells** (10) .
t02-23-1: 23. — Around the gymnasts, boys and girls are playing various **games**. The girls are playing with their **hoop** (14) ; they **skip** (13) , or invite their brothers and cousins to a game of **croquet** (15) . They love knocking their opponent’s **ball** away with their **wooden mallet**, just when he thinks he is going straight through the hoop!
t02-24-1: 24. — The boys prefer more strenuous games. They gladly play **ninepins** (16) , which they knock down neatly with the **ball** (17) . They do not turn up their noses at the **spinning top** (18) and **cup-and-ball** (19) , or even **toad in the hole** (20) . But their favourite games are **marbles** (21) and **fives** (22) , because the wall of the **greenhouse** (26) is just right for bouncing the light ball off.
t02-25-1: 25. — Little John, up on his **stilts** (24) , is very skilful and keeps his balance very well. Near him, a few friends are playing **hide-and-seek** (25) in that greenhouse and behind the **hedge**. Others prefer **hot cockles** (28) or **shuttlecock** (29) , which flits from one **racket** to the other.
t02-26-1: 26. — In the middle of the lawn there are two trees. At the foot of one of them, seven or eight boys have started a game of **shoulder-leap** (30) (*) . This game is not known in every country; but everyone knows what **leapfrog** is, which the children are not playing just now.
t02-27-1: 27. — **Blind man’s buff** (31) is also great fun; girls and boys take turns to put the **blindfold** over their eyes and catch the clumsy ones who let themselves be caught.
t02-28-1: 28. — In the middle of the lawn, here is a very French game, though a somewhat rough one: it is the **bear** (32) , far noisier than the peaceful game of the **kite** (33) or even than the English game of **tennis** (34) .
t02-29-1: 29. — That last sport is what the older pupils love best. Even our teachers are happy to join in. It calls for real skill and agility, and I love it. I leave the **swing** (35) to the girls.
t02-30-1: 30. — I am not keen on another English game that could easily turn dangerous.
t02-30-1b: I mean **football** (36) , which my older brother loves. I prefer our old game of **prisoner’s base** (38) , just as healthy and far less brutal.
t02-31-1: 31. — I also love riding round the lawn on a **bicycle** (37) .
t02-32-1: 32. — Next year I am going to learn to **ride** (39) . A horse is such a fine sight when it steps or trots gracefully, and clears the obstacles at a gallop!
t02-33-1: 33. — In summer we learn to **swim** (40) . We dive and bathe with delight in the clear, cool water of the river. Sometimes, at the end, we send up a paper **balloon** (41) , which rises majestically into the air as soon as it is filled with hot air.
t02-34-1: 34. — There are many other games as well, but I would never get to the end of the list, and you can see from this short account that Thursdays on our lawn are anything but dull.
t02-34-2: N.B. — *The teacher will easily fill out this chapter by describing each of the more important games in greater detail.*
t03-apar-2: (Charts 3 and 4 are arranged so as to present, in four **family scenes**, the essential vocabulary of the **weather**, **age**, the **family**, **clothing** and **health**.)
t03-c1-01-1: 1. — We are in **spring**, in the month of **March**, **April** or **May**, on a day of the **week** — **Monday**, **Tuesday** or **Wednesday**. It is **ten o’clock** in the morning.
t03-c1-02-1: 2. — The **weather** is fine, the **air** clear. The sun is shining. A few small **clouds** (2) are rising in the blue **sky** (1) .
t03-c1-03-1: 3. — The **trees** have hardly any **leaves**. The slender **poplars** (3) and the tall **plane tree** (17) still bear nothing but buds.
t03-c1-04-1: 4. — The **swallows** (4) are back, and they wheel with joyful cries around the **spire** (7) of the **bell tower** (5) that crowns the village **church** (6) .
t03-c1-05-1: 5. — This church is very plain, with its great **doorway** (13) and its big **clock** (8) . The small **hand** (9) is on the figure X: it marks the **hours**. The **big one** (10) is on XII (noon); it marks the **minutes**.
t03-c1-06-1: 6. — In the tower the **bells** (11) are ringing gaily. At the top of the roof stands a small stone **cross** (12) .
t03-c1-07-1: 7. — The church has not only a great **doorway** (13) , it also has a small side door. Through this door the **parish priest** (15) , in his **cassock**, comes out of the **vestry** (14) and makes his way to the **presbytery** (19) .
t03-c1-08-1: 8. — Next to him is the **milkwoman** (24) with her **donkey** (23) . She is on her way back from town, where she has delivered her good milk for the children.
t03-c1-09-1: 9. — Master Aliboron (the donkey) is quite pleased with this morning run. He breathes in with delight the air scented by the **blossom** (20) that covers the **fruit trees** (18) of the neighboring **orchard**. Those **peach trees** (18) and **apricot trees** (19) are all pink and white, and they promise a fine crop.
t03-c1-10-1: 10. — Meanwhile the little **bees** (22) from the **hive** (21) go there to gather their sweet **honey**, humming as they work.
t03-c1-11-1: 11. — But what is happening? Here come the village children, running up and scattering the frightened **geese** (25) . It is the procession leaving the church after the **christening** of the notary’s son.
t03-c1-12-1: 12. — Little James, in his **cradle** (26) , wakes at the joyful pealing of the bells, and his sister Madeleine, who wants to see the procession too, asks her mother to come and comb her hair and dress her on the doorstep.
t03-c1-13-1: 13. — Her mother agrees. She puts on her **headscarf** (28) , her **bodice** (29) and her **apron** (30) , and comes and sits on a little chair in front of the door. Madeleine has only her **petticoat** (31) and her **bodice** (32) .
t03-c1-14-1: 14. — How happy she is! She forgets her favourite flowers, her **carnations** (34) , where the **butterflies** (35) settle, her **tulips** (36) , her **lilies of the valley** (37) in their **pots** (38) on the **wall** (33) , and her **roses** (39) that make such a fine hedge. She is gazing at the rich clothes of the ladies in the procession.
t03-c1-15-1: 15. — The village boys pay little attention to the clothes. They rush forward and jostle one another to get **candy** (55) or **coins** (52) . One of them is crying (40) .
t03-c1-16-1: 16. — Another has trodden on the paw of the **dog** (42) , which runs off yelping and puts to flight the **hen** (43) and her **chicks** (44) .
t03-c1-17-1: 17. — At the head of the procession walks the **nurse** (45) . She has a fine **bonnet** (46) with long ribbons. She is carrying the **newborn baby** (47) , all dressed in **lace** (48) .
t03-c1-18-1: 18. — Behind the nurse come the **godfather** (49) and the **godmother** (53) . They are handing out the candy and the coins. The godfather has **gloves** (51) and a **top hat** (50) . The godmother is holding a fine **bouquet** (54) in her hand.
t03-c1-19-1: 19. — Behind them we can see the child’s **uncle** (56) and **aunt** (58) . The aunt has an elegant **hat** (59) , the uncle a black **frock coat** (57) and a white vest. Next come the **cousin** (60) and his **cousin** (61) . The latter is holding by the hand the newborn baby’s **sister** (62) , little Bertha.
t03-c1-20-1: 20. — Bertha’s other **brother** (63) walks behind. He is giving his hand to a **relative** (64) . The family’s **friends** (65) come after them.
t03-c1-21-1: 21. — Near the procession, a **beggar** (66) is leaning on his **crutch** (67) . He is asking for money.
t03-c1-22-1: 22. — On the other side is a very **polite** (68) little boy. He raises his cap and wishes **“good morning”** to the people he knows.
t03-c1-23-1: 23. — The villagers have come out of their houses to watch the christening procession go by. We can see a **countryman** (69) with his **cotton cap** and beside him a **countrywoman** (70) . Then an **old woman** (71) leaning on her **stick** (72) . Lastly the **miller** (73) with his broad **felt hat** (74) , and a young countrywoman in **clogs** (75) teaching her baby to walk.
t03-c1-24-1: 24. — It is a very lively scene.
t03-c2-01-1: 1. — **Summer** has come. The blazing sun of the month of **June** (**July** or **August**) tempts the young people to bathe and to go boating.
t03-c2-02-1: 2. — On the right bank of the river, the oarsmen are undressing to take part in the water sports and the regatta.
t03-c2-03-1: 3. — One of them is taking off his **shoes** (1) ; he is unlacing (unbuttoning) them. His two friends are already done. They now have nothing on but their **jersey** (2) and **bathing trunks** (3) . They are chatting as they wait for their friends. They are talking about the fair and the festival being held on the other bank.
t03-c2-04-1: 4. — On the ground near them lie their friends’ **clothes**: a **pair** of **boots** (4) , **shoes** (5) , **socks** (6) , **felt** (7) and **straw** (8) hats and a **tie** (9) .
t03-c2-05-1: 5. — One of the young men has carefully folded his **jacket** (10) . He is laying it on a towel, in which his neighbor will shortly wrap up both their **suits**.
t03-c2-06-1: 6. — A sixth boy is running late. He still has his **cap** (11) on his head. He has taken off neither his **shirt** (12) , nor his **collar** (13) , nor his **cuffs** (14) . He is holding his **vest** (17) in his hand and still has his **trousers** (16) and **suspenders** (15) on. He will certainly not be ready for the next race.
t03-c2-07-1: 7. — Near the young men, a path lined with **thistles** (18) leads down to the riverside, where old James is getting ready, among the **reeds** (19) , the **fireworks** (20) that will be set off in the evening.
t03-c2-08-1: 8. — On the river, a few ladies sheltering under their parasols are out in a **rowing boat** (21) . They are following the race, which is very exciting. In each **skiff** (22) , four **rowers** (24) are pulling with all their strength, while the **coxswain** (26) holds the **rudder** (25) and steers the fragile craft. The **oars** (23) strike the water in time, and the light boats race along at a dizzying speed.
t03-c2-09-1: 9. — A few young men are competing, near the pier of the bridge, for the prize of the **greasy pole** (28) . One of them is edging carefully along the springy, slippery pole to reach the little **flag** (29) fixed at the end. His luckless **rival** (30) has fallen into the water. He is swimming back to shore.
t03-c2-10-1: 10. — Older lads are **water-jousting** (32) near the **quay** (33) . A large **crowd** (31) is watching all these games, leaning on the **parapet** of the **bridge** (27) and packed along the **bank**. A few onlookers, though, are turning round to follow the game of the **climbing pole** (45) , or to admire the **mayoral procession** on its way to the **prize-giving**.
t03-c2-11-1: 11. — First come a few **urchins** (35) running ahead of the **band** (36) ; then come the **mayor** (37) , his deputies and the **town council** of the little town. Last of all march the **firemen** (38) .
t03-c2-12-1: 12. — There is a great crowd on the **fairground** (39) . People come to see the various **booths**: the **merry-go-round** (40) , the **circus** (41) , where the performance has already begun; the **public dance** (42) , where the young men and women of the town are enjoying themselves **dancing**.
t03-c2-13-1: 13. — At the far end we can see the **arena** (44) , where the brave Spanish **matador** fights the furious **bull** (45) ; then the **roller coaster** (49) and the **shooting gallery** (46) , where people practice handling **firearms** and shooting at the **target**.
t03-c2-14-1: 14. — Close by stands the **fairground theater** (47) , where **comedy** and **drama** are performed. Very near it stands the booth of the **giant** (48) and the **dwarf**. The **height** of the first is two meters fifteen; the second is barely as tall as a child.
t03-c2-15-1: 15. — Lastly there is the great **menagerie** (50) with its **wild animals**, its **tiger** (51) with its powerful **claws**, its **lion** (52) with its thick **mane**, its two **giraffes** (53) and its **elephant** (54) , which uses its **trunk** so cleverly.
t03-c2-16-1: 16. — The **tamer** (55) who trains these animals is standing at the door of the booth.
t04-apar-1: CHART No. 4 Middle Age and Old Age.
t04-c1-01-1: 1. — The young people have grown up. One of them, John, is getting married. We are at the **wedding breakfast**, which brings the families of the bride and groom together around the same table.
t04-c1-02-1: 2. — We are in **fall**, in the month of **September**. The cold wind of **October** and **November** has not yet stripped the countryside of its green leaves. The evening air is mild and fragrant; so dinner is being served under the **veranda** (8) that opens on to the garden.
t04-c1-03-1: 3. — In the distance, on the **hill** (3) , stands the home of John’s parents, an elegant **country house** (1) hidden in the greenery; fine vineyards, which yield an excellent wine, cover the slope of the hillside. The winegrower looks after them.

t05-01-1: John. — Uncle, I would really like to know how a **house** is built.
t05-01-2: The Uncle (80) . — That’s easy enough, my boy. Come with me and I’ll show you the one Mr Bernard (79) is having built, the one I’m going to live in.
t05-01-3: John. — And who drew the **plan** (76) of this house?
t05-01-4: The Uncle. — The **architect** (75) ; he drew it up very clearly, it was approved, and the **building contractor** (77) started work.
t05-01-5: John. — And who is the contractor?
t05-01-6: The Uncle. — Mr White, the father of your friend James. He runs the site along with Mr Roux, the architect.
t05-01-7: Well, look at that! Here comes Mr White at just the right moment with his **rule** (78) , and Mr Roux with his plan.
t05-01-8: Good morning, gentlemen. How are you?
t05-01-9: Mr Roux. — Very well, thanks. Morning, John — hasn’t he grown!
t05-01-10: The Uncle. — He has, hasn’t he. He’s quite the little man now. He is very serious; everything he sees has to be explained to him. Today he would like to know how a house is built.
t05-01-11: Mr White. — Come along with me, then, and I’ll explain it to you right now. I do like children who want to learn.
t05-01-12: You see that workman with a **shovel** (82) in his hand: he is a **navvy** (81) . He is digging a **trench** (46) to lay the water pipe. He also dug out the ground where the house stands, so that the bricklayer could put up the four **walls**. The part of those walls that is in the ground is called the **foundations** (2) . The space enclosed by the foundations forms the **cellar** (3) . This cellar has a small window called an **air vent** (5) , a **door** (4) and a stairway.
t05-01-13: The **bricklayer** (108) went on raising the walls, leaving openings for the **doors** (8) and the **windows** (17) .
t05-01-14: John. — But I can’t see him, this bricklayer!
t05-01-15: Mr White. — He has finished working on the house now. He is over by the **stable** (54) , up on his **scaffolding** (110) , building the wall of the **wash house** (56) .
t05-01-16: He has a trowel, a trough and a **plumb line** (109) . But you won’t remember those names.
t05-01-17: John. — Oh yes I will, because I’m going to ask my uncle for a little trowel and a trough, and I’ll make a plumb line myself with a piece of string.
t05-01-18: The Uncle. — Ah, very good. But tell me, John, what do you need to build a house?
t05-01-20: The Uncle. — Exactly. Look at that man in the big hat, on his **cart** (136) . He is a **carter** (135) . Every day he brings **blocks of stone** (60) here. He unloads his cart in the yard, and the **stonecutters** (83) dress the blocks and saw them with their **stone saw** (85) . A **labourer** (146) carries them to the bricklayer, who sets them in place.
t05-01-21: Meanwhile the **mortar mixer** (87) is preparing the mortar. He needs **sand** (62) , **lime** (63) and **water** (64) . The lime is beside him in a **sack** (71) ; a **bricklayer’s mate** (111) brings him the sand in a **wheelbarrow** (112) , and the **apprentice** (113) is at the pump (58) . He is filling a **bucket** (114) . The mortar will soon be ready. The **hod carrier** (107) takes it and carries it up the ladder to the scaffolding, where a bricklayer is finishing that side of the house.
t05-01-22: And now, what do you call the workman who makes the **roof** (31) ?
t05-01-24: Mr White. — Yes, but first comes the **carpenter** (115) .
t05-01-25: The carpenter makes the **roof frame** (35) . He joins the **beams** (37) with **pegs** (117) . Those workmen up there, in their wide velvet breeches, are carpenters. One is holding a small beam and the other is cutting a peg with his **axe** (116) . The one near the **chimney** (41) is the roofer. He nails laths on to the **joists** (*) , and **slates** (66) on to the laths. Sometimes he lays tiles.
t05-01-26: The roof of the stable is **tiled** (55) , that of the house is **slated** (32) , and that of the veranda is of **zinc** (24) .
t05-01-27: John. — Does the roofer make the zinc roofs as well?
t05-01-28: Mr White. — No, that’s the **zinc worker** (121) or the **plumber**, the one setting a **dormer window** (38) into the roof of the house. He also lays the **roof gutters** (43) and the **downpipes** (42) . He solders the zinc and the tinplate. He is the one who fixed the **lightning conductor** (40) and the **weathervane** (39) on the **gable** (36) .
t05-01-29: John. — Is the house finished, then?
t05-01-30: Mr White. — Not quite. The **plasterer** (99) builds with **bricks** (61) the partitions that divide it into the different rooms. He lays **plaster** (70) on the **ceilings** (26) and on the walls. Just now he is working on the ceiling of the **veranda** (33) . Like the bricklayer, he has a **trowel** (100) and a **trough** (101) .
t05-01-31: Then the joiner makes the doors, the windows, the **wooden floors** (16) and the **shutters** (19) .
t05-01-32: Just now he is working in the yard at his **workbench** (90) . He has a **saw** (94) to cut the **wood** (69) , a **plane** (91) , a **holdfast** (92) , a **chisel** (94 *bis*) , a **pair of compasses** (95) and a wooden **mallet** (95 *bis*) .
t05-01-33: John. — Oh, but being a joiner is even more fun than being a bricklayer. Uncle, will you buy me a workbench, a saw and a plane? I’m going to make a kennel for Medor.
t05-01-35: John. — Oh, thank you! And who’s that man standing near the front door?
t05-01-36: Mr White. — He is a **painter** (102) . He is standing on his ladder with a pot of **paint** (103) and his **brush** (104) . He is coating the wood of the front door so that it will last longer.
t05-01-37: He is also the one who hangs the wallpaper in the rooms.
t05-01-38: The **upholsterer** (107) on a **ladder** (106) , out on the **balcony** (28) , is putting up a **blind** (29) .
t05-01-39: The workman standing by the big window is the **glazier** (96) . He fixes the **panes** (18) with **putty** (73) . That other workman, kneeling by the cellar door, is a **locksmith** (97) . He is fitting a **lock** (6) . His **file** (98) is beside him.
t05-01-40: John. — Is the man hitting a piece of iron with his **hammer** (84) a locksmith too?
t05-01-41: Mr White. — Not quite — he’s a **blacksmith** (125) . He is forging **ironwork** (67) for the **electrician** (124) , who is on the roof of the **coach house** (51) . He has a **forge** (126) , an **anvil** (127) and a pair of **tongs** (128) .
t05-01-42: The electrician is fixing the **copper wire** (44) of the telephone.
t05-01-43: The Uncle. — At the far end of the **yard** (45) , near the **railings** (47) and the **carriage gate** (48) , you can see the **gardener** (129) . He is getting the little **garden** (49) ready. He has dug the soil over with his **spade** (131) , he is sowing seed and raking with the **rake** (130) . Then, with his **watering can** (132) , he will water the **flower beds** (50) and the plants will grow.
t05-01-44: The **groom** (133) , who has just tended the horse and fed it, is cleaning the **carriage** (52) with a sponge, a **hand pump** (134) and a bucket of water. Then he will put it away in the coach house and shut the door with the heavy **bolt** (53) .
t05-01-45: There, I hope you are satisfied now — you have had plenty of explanations.
t05-01-46: John. — Yes, uncle, but I’d like to see the inside of the house.
t05-01-47: The Uncle. — That can wait for tomorrow. Mr Roux will explain the plan to you and tell you the name of each room.
t05-01-48: The Architect. — Come along, John, I’m going to take you round the different parts of the house.
t05-01-49: Let’s go in on the **ground floor** (7) . Here is the **doorbell** button (11) . We climb the three **steps** (14) of the **front steps** (9) , we cross the **threshold** (10) of the **front door** (8) , and here we are at the foot of the **staircase** (13) .
t05-01-51: The Architect. — No, this is the **hall** (12) . The **corridor** (a) is at the far end. On the right, here are the **drawing room** (b) and the **dining room** (c) ; opposite the dining room are the **kitchen** (d) and the **pantry** (e) ; then, at the front, the **study** (f) . The **veranda** (23) , with its **glazed door** (25) , is next to the drawing room.
t05-01-52: Now we’ll go up the stairs. Hold on to the **handrail** (15) and count the steps. There are fourteen. Here is the **landing** (m) : we are on the first **floor** (27) .
t05-01-53: Opposite the stairs are the **lavatory** (20) and the **dressing room** (j) . On the right, a fine **bedroom** (g) with two windows on the **front** (1) of the house. On the left are the **bathroom** (1) and the **guest room** (i) with a large **alcove** (h) . Next to the bedroom is the **children’s room** (k) . It opens on to a wide **terrace** (21) . Under this terrace is another lavatory (20) , and against the wall, here is the **bell** (22) that is rung for dinner.
t05-01-54: John. — Let’s go up to the **second floor**.
t05-01-55: The Architect. — There is no second floor. Under the roof there are only **attic rooms** (33) and the loft (34) . That is the whole tour — we can go back down.
t05-01-56: John. — Thank you, sir, that was really interesting. I’m going to tell my father everything I have seen.
